1.title: The AI/ML Lifecycle, MLOps and Metrics
1.text: Welcome to Module three: the A I and M L Lifecycle, M L Ops and Metrics. This module covers task statement one point three. You will follow a model from business goal to monitoring, learn where models come from and how they run in production, see which A W S services fit each stage, and learn the metrics that tell you whether a model is good.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Describe the phases of the M L lifecycle and how they differ. Name the sources of models: open source, provider models and custom training. Compare managed A P I and self-hosted A P I ways to run a model. Match A W S services to each stage of the pipeline. And explain M L Ops, and read accuracy, precision, recall and F one, together with business metrics.

1.title: Case Check-In: Cedar and Salt Plans a Cancellation Model
1.text: Cedar and Salt Travel loses money on late cancellations, so the team wants a cancellation-risk model. Before any code, the leaders ask three things: what are the steps, where does the model come from, and how will we run it? They also ask how they will know it is good, in model terms and in money terms. Your job is to walk the team through the lifecycle, the services, M L Ops and the metrics.

1.title: The ML Lifecycle at a Glance
1.text: Here is the M L lifecycle. The figure shows six phases. One, business goal: the problem and the value to gain. Two, problem framing: turn it into an M L problem, with a target to predict. Three, data processing: collect, prepare and engineer features. Four, model development: train, tune and evaluate. Five, deployment: make predictions in production. And six, monitoring: check performance over time, then loop back. Exam tip: the phases are a cycle, not a straight line, because monitoring feeds new data and retraining.

1.title: Business Goal and Problem Framing
1.text: The first two phases come before any data work. In business goal, you state the problem and the value to be gained, with measurable success criteria. In problem framing, you say what is observed and what should be predicted: the label, or target. You also decide how performance and error will be measured, and you check first that M L is the right tool, as Module two explained. At Cedar and Salt, the goal is to predict whether a booking will be canceled, to cut empty rooms. Exam tip: starting with the business goal is the first step; data and models come later.

1.title: Data Processing: Collect, Prepare and Engineer Features
1.text: Data processing has three jobs. Collect data from many sources into one place, often Amazon S three. Prepare it: clean errors, fix inconsistent values and handle missing data. Then engineer features, which means creating, transforming and selecting the variables the model learns from. Data quality sets the ceiling for model quality. Finally, split the data: most goes to train, and the rest goes to validate and test. Exam tip: poor data gives a poor model, however good the algorithm.

1.title: Model Development: Train, Tune and Evaluate
1.text: Model development has three steps. Train: an algorithm learns from the training data to produce a model. Tune: adjust settings, called hyperparameters, to improve results; specialists do this, and the exam does not test it in depth. Evaluate: measure quality on data the model has not seen, using metrics. A C I C D pipeline can automate build, train and release. Training can start from an algorithm, or from a pre-trained base model. Exam tip: always evaluate on data the model did not train on.

1.title: Deployment and Monitoring
1.text: After development comes deployment and monitoring. Deploy the model so applications can request inferences. Then monitor it, because performance can degrade as the world changes. Drift means the data, or the relationship the model learned, has shifted. When quality drops, collect new data and retrain. At Cedar and Salt, travel patterns change by season, so the model must be watched. Exam tip: deployment is not the end; a model needs monitoring and retraining.

1.title: Where Models Come From
1.text: Where do models come from? There are three sources. Open-source pre-trained models are publicly available models you can use, adapt or fine-tune; on A W S they appear in the SageMaker JumpStart model hub. Provider models are foundation models from A W S and other companies, used through an A P I; on A W S that is Amazon Bedrock. Custom-trained models are ones you train on your own data, with SageMaker A I. As of the fifth of November, twenty twenty-six, Bedrock lists more than one hundred models from providers including Amazon, Anthropic, DeepSeek, OpenAI and x A I. Exam tip: starting from a pre-trained model is faster and cheaper than training from scratch.

1.title: Ways to Use a Model in Production
1.text: There are two main ways to use a model in production. A managed A P I service means A W S runs the model and scales it, and you call an A P I, for example with Amazon Bedrock or a SageMaker A I endpoint. That is less work, with less control. A self-hosted A P I means you run the model on your own compute, such as Amazon E C two, E C S or E K S, and expose your own A P I. That gives more control, with more to operate. Choose managed to move fast with a small team, and self-hosted for custom runtimes or special control needs. Exam tip: no servers to manage means a managed A P I service, and full control of the stack means a self-hosted A P I.

1.title: AWS Services by Stage of the Pipeline
1.text: Here are A W S services by stage of the pipeline. For data: Amazon S three, A W S Glue, Glue DataBrew for no-code cleaning, A W S Data Exchange for third-party data, Amazon E M R and Amazon Redshift. To build and train: Amazon SageMaker A I and Amazon Bedrock, and Kiro, an A I-powered development environment, to write the application code. To deploy: SageMaker A I endpoints and Bedrock, or Amazon E C two, E C S or E K S for self-hosting. To use the results: Amazon Quick, an A I companion for research, business insights and automation. To monitor: SageMaker Model Monitor and Amazon CloudWatch. Exam tip: match the stage to the service: data prep, build, deploy, use, monitor.

2.title: MLOps: What and Why
2.text: M L Ops applies DevOps ideas to M L, so that models reach production reliably. It includes experimentation: try and track many versions. It includes repeatable processes: automate pipelines instead of one-off notebooks. It includes scalable systems that handle more data and requests. It includes managing technical debt and reaching production readiness. And it includes model monitoring and re-training when performance drops. Exam tip: M L Ops is about repeatable, monitored delivery of models, not a single tool.

2.title: MLOps on Amazon SageMaker AI
2.text: SageMaker A I has a capability for each M L Ops need. To track and compare experiments, use SageMaker Experiments. To automate the workflow, use SageMaker A I Workflows, also called Pipelines. To version and approve models, use the Model Registry. To follow what produced a model, use M L Lineage Tracking. To watch a live model, use Model Monitor. And to set up C I C D for M L, use SageMaker Projects. Exam tip: to version a model, use Model Registry; to watch it in production, use Model Monitor.

2.title: Model Performance Metrics
2.text: Now the model metrics. Accuracy is the share of correct predictions out of all predictions: the overall hit rate. Precision asks, of the items predicted positive, how many really are positive: few false alarms. Recall asks, of the real positives, how many were found: few misses. And the F one score is the balance of precision and recall, as one combined number. A U C summarizes how well a classifier separates the classes across thresholds, though it goes beyond the guide. Exam tip: precision cares about false positives, and recall cares about false negatives.

2.title: Precision or Recall?
2.text: How do you choose? If you want to flag every booking likely to cancel, a miss, or false negative, is the costly mistake, so favor recall. If you want to send a costly retention offer only to real risks, a false alarm, or false positive, is the costly mistake, so favor precision. To keep both in balance, use the F one score. And when one class is rare, accuracy can mislead, so look at precision, recall or F one. Exam tip: accuracy alone can hide problems when one class is rare.

2.title: Business Metrics for an ML Model
2.text: A model can score well and still not pay off, so measure business value too. Useful business metrics include cost per user or per prediction, development costs and running costs, customer feedback and satisfaction, and return on investment, or R O I. Always compare the model's value with the cost to build and run it. Exam tip: F one and accuracy are model metrics, and R O I and cost per user are business metrics.

2.title: What the Exam Asks: The Lifecycle, MLOps and Metrics
2.text: Here is how the exam frames this module. Which phase: business goal, framing, data processing, model development, deployment or monitoring. Which source: open-source pre-trained, provider model or custom-trained. Which way to run: a managed A P I service or a self-hosted A P I. Which service: S three, Glue DataBrew, Data Exchange, SageMaker A I, Bedrock or Model Monitor. Which M L Ops idea: repeatable, scalable, monitored or retrained. And which metric: accuracy, precision, recall, F one, or a business metric. Exam tip: name the phase or the need first, then the service or metric.

2.title: Design Check: Cedar and Salt's Cancellation Model
2.text: Now a design check, with an ordering. Cover the right column and name the phase for each step. One, cut empty rooms from late cancellations: business goal. Two, predict canceled or not: problem framing. Three, clean and prepare past bookings: data processing. Four, train and evaluate with F one: model development. Five, call it from the booking site: deployment. Six, watch for seasonal drift and retrain: monitoring. Then match a metric to each worry. Missed cancellations need recall. Wasted offers need precision. And payback needs R O I. Pause the video if you want more time.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. The lifecycle runs from business goal, to problem framing, data processing, model development, deployment and monitoring. Models come from open-source pre-trained models, provider models and custom training. You run a model through a managed A P I service or a self-hosted A P I. M L Ops means experimentation, repeatable and scalable processes, monitoring and retraining. And the metrics are accuracy, precision, recall and F one, plus business metrics such as R O I.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Which sequence lists the phases of the M L lifecycle in the correct order? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: business goal, problem framing, data processing, model development, deployment and monitoring. The lifecycle starts with the business goal, then frames the problem, processes the data, develops the model, deploys it and monitors it, with feedback loops back to earlier phases.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Cedar and Salt's small team wants its booking site to call the cancellation model through an A P I, without managing servers or scaling. Which approach fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B, a managed A P I service, such as a SageMaker A I endpoint. It runs and scales the model for you, so the team calls an A P I and manages no servers. A self-hosted A P I gives more control, but you run and scale the compute yourself.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Select two. Which two are fundamental M L Ops concepts? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and B. M L Ops stresses repeatable, automated processes, experiment tracking, scalable systems, managing technical debt, and monitoring with re-training. The other options describe habits that M L Ops tries to remove.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Missing a booking that will actually be canceled is very costly, so the team wants to find as many real cancellations as possible. Which metric should it favor? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A, recall. It measures how many of the real positives the model finds, so it is the metric to favor when misses are costly. Precision penalizes false alarms, and the other options do not measure classification quality.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. An analyst with no coding skills wants to clean and normalize raw booking data visually before it is used for M L. Which A W S service fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C, A W S Glue DataBrew. It is a visual data preparation tool that cleans and normalizes data without code. Data Exchange finds third-party data, Rekognition analyzes images, and Polly turns text into speech.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Which of the following is a business metric for evaluating an M L model, rather than a model performance metric? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D, return on investment. It compares the value an M L solution brings with its cost, so it is a business metric. The F one score, precision and recall measure how well a model predicts.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all six answers. Question one: D. Question two: B. Question three: A and B. Question four: A. Question five: C. Question six: D. That completes Module three, and the first domain. Next, Module four opens the domain on generative A I with its core concepts: tokens, embeddings, foundation models and the first ideas behind agents.
